newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: De Beers mulls protecting sold-off plots.
newsitem.headline: De Beers mulls protecting sold-off plots.

text.p: De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd said on Friday it was mulling action to prevent foreign diamond mining companies from snapping up mining properties sold to black South Africans.

De Beers diamond consultant Gareth Penny told the parliamentary minerals and energy committee that the group had reviewed all its mining properties earlier this year and identified 50 that were suitable for small black-owned mining companies.
"We put those out for sale earlier this year and we were very pleased that we managed to sell 44," Penny said.
"But we were a little disappointed that one, maybe more, of the properties that we sold...have in fact been on-sold to Canadian companies."
This had created unwelcome competition and De Beers was now considering introducing a buy-back clause on property sold, the company said.
"It worries us because we think that in the new South Africa, we should not only have skilled people but also entrepreneurs," projects manager Raisaka Masebelanga told the committee.
Minerals and Energy Minister Penuell Maduna recently criticised large mining groups for monopolising mineral rights and sitting on properties rather than developing them.
Maduna hinted that he might change the present system of mineral rights to ensure that more black groups became involved in mining.
Penny and Masebelanga defended De Beers' diamond buying and selling cartel, the Central Selling Organisation (CSO), saying that it had brought stability to the diamond market.
The decision by Australia's Argyle diamond mine to pull out of the CSO last year had depressed the market for the type of diamonds produced by Argyle.
"It is putting a lot of pressure, particularly on the more marginal mines and also on the viability of retreating dumps." Penny said.

Committee members claimed that De Beers was not doing enough to support social programmes in South Africa, and one accused it of supporting child labour in Indian diamond cutting factories which De Beers supplied with diamonds.
Penny said that research had shown that De Beers in fact spent four times as much on social programmes as similar companies in Britain.
